identification.name: Nitinol (NiTi Shape Memory Alloy)
identification.common_form_notes: Most commonly supplied as fine wire, which isn't well represented by this database's form options — treat Round Bar/Tube as the closest available approximations. Conventional machining is difficult: Nitinol work-hardens rapidly and its superelastic springback resists clean cutting, so wire forming, laser cutting, grinding, and EDM are far more common than milling/turning. The defining process step ("shape setting") is a constrained heat treatment (typically ~500°C) that trains the material to "remember" a target shape — not captured by any fabrication_processes option here.
identification.notes: A "smart material" comparison/inspiration entry, not something a capstone team would typically source and machine themselves without specialized shape-setting equipment and expertise. This is the shape-memory-effect grade (as opposed to the separate superelastic grade also in this database): deform in the low-temperature martensite phase, then heat above the austenite finish temperature (Af) to recover the original "trained" shape — directly useful for thermally-triggered actuators, valves, and self-deploying structures (this specific grade's "High-Temperature" designation means its Af is set above room/body temperature, so it stays in its deformed shape until deliberately heated). IMPORTANT DATA GAP: this source (a compact MatWeb datasheet) does not report the Af transformation temperature or elastic modulus — both checked directly and not found, and a supplementary search of a Goodfellow technical overview didn't yield grade-specific numbers either, only general alloy-family ranges: Young's modulus ~20–50 GPa in the martensite phase vs. ~40–90 GPa in the austenite phase (a defining, dramatic stiffness difference between phases, unlike any other metal in this database) and Af typically −20°C to +110°C depending on composition (0.1 at% Ni shift moves Ms (martensite start temperature) by 10–15°C). Young's modulus is left null here rather than picking an arbitrary point in that wide range. Elongation at break (12%, stored as ductility) is distinct from the source's separately-reported "max strain recovery" of 8% — the latter is the shape-memory-specific recoverable strain (how much deformation can be imposed and still fully recovered on heating), not simple ductility; both figures are real but represent different concepts. Nitinol is generally weakly paramagnetic (not ferromagnetic) — a practically important property since it makes Nitinol medical devices MRI-compatible, unlike the ferromagnetic martensitic steels elsewhere in this database — MRI stands for magnetic resonance imaging. Shear strength is not derived via von Mises — Nitinol's transformation-based deformation mechanism doesn't behave like a conventional ductile metal yielding by dislocation slip, so the standard derivation used elsewhere in this database isn't clearly applicable here.

typical_usage: Thermally-triggered actuators, self-deploying structures (aerospace antenna masts, solar array hinges), and thermal-fuse/trigger mechanisms exploiting the shape-memory effect — deform cold, recover shape when heated past the transformation temperature. Also used for fire-safety releases, couplings, and connectors that need to actuate at a specific temperature without electronics.
